unlisted_practices: Regulators should publish open and transparent clinical evaluation data for AI medical devices, ideally mandated, including trial protocols and outcomes.
Regulators should publish a minimum public dataset for every approved AI medical device, with metadata indicating any withheld information.
Regulators should develop AI-specific nomenclature, building on existing systems such as GMDN, to identify and categorise AI medical devices.
Regulators should adopt structured, machine-readable database formats with standard identifiers such as UDI so devices can be tracked across jurisdictions and versions.
Regulators should co-design regulatory databases with diverse stakeholders, defining required information, update frequency, technical detail, and public-facing content.
Regulators should link regulatory approval, clinical evaluation, and post-market surveillance data in unified or interoperable databases.
Regulators should federate regulatory databases across jurisdictions via secure APIs exchanging standardised metadata, while retaining sovereignty over sensitive data.
Regulators should analyse post-market data through federated analytics pipelines to detect emerging safety signals and performance drift in near real time.
Regulators, manufacturers, and health systems should share dashboards of key metrics such as recall frequency and bias indicators to support transparent public reporting.
Regulators and policymakers should strengthen incentives and invest in regulatory infrastructure for ongoing real-world performance monitoring and lifecycle data generation.
Regulators should harmonise and systematise adverse event and performance reporting practices for AI medical devices across jurisdictions.
Stakeholders should agree shared ontologies and a minimum common data model for regulatory databases through mechanisms such as IMDRF.
Manufacturers should share ongoing performance and safety data of AI medical devices efficiently and rapidly across jurisdictions and stakeholders.
